title: Log-concavity transitions in sums of polynomial powers
oneLine: A hub joined to m three-vertex paths has log-concave independent-set counts exactly when m ≤ 16,391, so four is the least diameter at which a tree can fail log-concavity, and at that diameter runs of failures can be arbitrarily long.
abstract: Count the independent sets of each size in a graph (sets of vertices with no two adjacent). For trees this sequence was long expected to be log-concave (each term squared at least the product of its neighbours), which would settle the open question of Alavi, Malde, Schwenk and Erdős whether it is unimodal. Non-log-concave trees have been known since 2023 (Kadrawi and Levit, 26 vertices), and later work gave many failures and arbitrarily long runs of consecutive failures (Galvin; Bautista-Ramos and coauthors; Yu, in an unrefereed archive), but every structured example has diameter six or more, while trees of diameter at most three are always log-concave (Galvin and Hilyard). This candidate studies the tree T_m obtained by joining a hub to the middle vertex of each of m disjoint three-vertex paths: 3m+1 vertices, diameter four. Its sequence is log-concave if and only if m ≤ 16,391; T_16,392, with 49,177 vertices, fails at exactly one place. For every m from 16,392 to 10^6, and for all sufficiently large m, the failures form one nonempty block, of length (2/log(3/2)) log log m + O(1) ≈ 4.93 log log m, with both ends located to within o(1) by explicit equations. Hence four is the least diameter of a non-log-concave tree and of a family with arbitrarily long runs. An exhaustive search finds no failing diameter-four tree with at most 62 vertices. A general theorem gives the same picture for (1+x)^{dm} + xP(x)^m whenever P has only negative real roots, P(0) = 1, leading coefficient at least 1 and P′(0) > d; the mechanism is the crossing of two Poisson-like coefficient tails. Limits: the runs are short and near the top of the sequence, so nothing follows about unimodality; the threshold is computer-assisted (exact integer arithmetic); general thresholds are not effective. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem 2.4 (computer-assisted proof): the independent set sequence of T_m (a hub joined to the middle vertices of m disjoint three-vertex paths) is log-concave if and only if m ≤ 16,391; the only failure of T_16,392 (49,177 vertices) is at reflected index 20; for 16,392 ≤ m ≤ 10^6 the failures form one nonempty block.

Theorem 2.3 (proof): for all sufficiently large m the failures of T_m form one nonempty block between explicit endpoints ℓ_m and u_m, with ℓ_m²(3/2)^{ℓ_m} = 18m and u_m = log_{3/2}(m/2), of length (2 log log m − log(36λ²))/λ + θ_m, λ = log(3/2), limsup|θ_m| ≤ 1; so about 4.93 log log m.
Corollary 2.5 (proof): four is the least diameter of a non-log-concave tree, and of a family of trees with unbounded runs of failures; one fixed three-vertex module repeated at one vertex suffices.

Proposition 2.6 (computer-assisted proof): every tree of diameter at most four with at most 62 vertices is log-concave, so the least order of a non-log-concave diameter-four tree lies between 63 and 49,177.

Theorem 2.1 (proof): if P has only negative real roots, P(0) = 1, leading coefficient at least 1 and P′(0) > d, the failures of (1+x)^{dm} + xP(x)^m eventually form one block of length (2/log r) log log m + O(1), r = P′(0)/d; the binomial case never fails.

narration: When do trees stop being smooth? An Evidence Press briefing. Take any network, and call a set of its nodes independent when no two of them are joined. Now count the independent sets of each size. For trees, which are networks without loops, these counts were long expected to rise and then fall smoothly. The precise form of that smoothness is called log-concavity: each count, squared, is at least the product of its two neighbours. Physicists meet the same numbers in a model of particles that cannot sit side by side. Since twenty twenty-three we have known that some trees break this rule. Later work found many breaks, and long runs of breaks in a row, but every structured example was a fairly deep tree, with diameter six or more. Shallower trees, of diameter three or less, never break the rule at all. This release asks how shallow a failing tree can be. The answer comes from a very simple shape. Take a central hub, and attach it to the middle of many short paths of three nodes, which the paper calls cherries. With up to sixteen thousand three hundred and ninety-one cherries, the counts stay smooth. Add one more cherry, and the tree breaks the rule in exactly one place. From then on the tree keeps failing, and wherever this has been settled, up to a million cherries and for all very large trees, the failures form a single unbroken block that grows extremely slowly. So the smallest diameter at which a tree can fail is four, and at that diameter runs of failures can be as long as you like. The reason is a tug of war. The counts split into two parts, depending on whether the hub is used, and each part on its own is smooth. Where the two parts are equally large, their sum is a mixture, and such mixtures are not smooth. The limits matter. The runs are short and sit near the very top of the sequence, so they say nothing about whether every tree rises and then falls. The exact threshold rests on a computer-assisted proof in exact arithmetic, with the scripts included. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, published on the fifteenth of November twenty twenty-six. Its review was internal and AI-assisted, not peer review. The paper and its evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.
